blocks.title: Why Model Context Protocol matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: An IDE assistant needs a standard way to read docs, tickets, and repo state through approved connectors. The learner's job is not to memorize Model Context Protocol; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved tool-call success rate across clients.

Running case: MCP server contract for docs search and ticket lookup. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: Model Context Protocol matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Model Context Protocol matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure tool-call success rate across clients on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: MCP server contract for docs search and ticket lookup

spans.text: Scenario: An IDE assistant needs a standard way to read docs, tickets, and repo state through approved connectors. The team wants to improve tool-call success rate across clients, but it has already seen this failure: each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Request: "A returning customer asks about a refund and mentions that they prefer email updates." The agent may remember the communication preference, but it must not store payment fragments, one-time codes, or raw complaint text longer than needed.

Artifact: MCP server contract for docs search and ticket lookup. It contains a memory schema, a write filter, retrieval rules, an escalation rule, and a tiny acceptance test tied to tool-call success rate across clients.

Worked output: store {customer_id, preference: "email updates", source: "support chat", expires_at: "90 days"}; reject {card digits, passwords, medical details}; retrieve only when the current task is about support follow-up.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: agent designer. Context: An IDE assistant needs a standard way to read docs, tickets, and repo state through approved connectors. Task: design MCP server contract for docs search and ticket lookup. Include memory or state fields, tool permissions, retrieval rules, human review points, audit logs, and failure tests. Output: {state, allowed_actions, blocked_actions, checks, metric}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Model Context Protocol to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

spans.text: Core workflow opens the machinery behind Model Context Protocol. In the running case, the important question is: what exactly changes between the user's request and the final output?
Mechanism means tracking what the agent observes, remembers, decides, acts on, and writes back to state.
Two framings for the same idea

items.text: Plain framing: imagine a reviewer following a checklist. They need to see what came in, what was considered, what was rejected, and why the final answer is safe to use.
Technical framing: imagine a trace. It should expose inputs, state, external evidence, model or algorithm output, validation result, and owner for exceptions.

blocks.title: Runnable check: filter memory before writing it
blocks.code:
# Model Context Protocol: memory write gate for the running case.
items = [
    {"kind": "preference", "text": "prefers email updates"},
    {"kind": "secret", "text": "card ends in 4242"},
    {"kind": "task_fact", "text": "refund requested for invoice INV-19"},
]
allowed = {"preference", "task_fact"}

def memory_write_candidates(items):
    return [item for item in items if item["kind"] in allowed]

kept = memory_write_candidates(items)
print([item["kind"] for item in kept])
print("safe to write" if len(kept) == 2 else "review")

spans.text: This is a runnable miniature, not the whole production system. It makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision rule, output, and a check related to each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the list of kept item kinds and the final decision.
predictThenReveal.answer:
It prints:
['preference', 'task_fact']
safe to write

The secret is filtered out before memory write. The point is not this tiny classifier; it is the boundary: memory should have an explicit write policy.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to MCP server contract for docs search and ticket lookup: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: tool-call success rate across clients becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Model Context Protocol design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: The agent remembers the wrong thing, forgets the important thing, or cannot distinguish user preference from sensitive data.
A tool call succeeds technically but changes real-world state without review.
The loop repeats because state was not updated after the last action.
The broad warning sign: tool-call success rate across clients gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

blocks.useWhen: Use the production path when tool-call success rate across clients affects users, trust, safety, cost, or compliance.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect: each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Make the failure visible before making the system more sophisticated.

buildOrder.label: Production checklist
buildOrder.detail: Reconstruct the lesson from memory and apply it without scaffolding.

checklist.label: Can you state the concrete user problem without buzzwords?
Does the artifact show input, evidence or state, decision, output, and owner?
Can you measure tool-call success rate across clients on realistic cases?
Does a test reproduce this failure: each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions?
Is the next rung clear after the first reliable version?

capstone.prompt: Create a one-page release-ready plan for MCP server contract for docs search and ticket lookup. Include: the user problem, realistic input, mechanism, design choice, runnable or reviewable check, metric (tool-call success rate across clients), failure case (each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions), owner, and the next rung after this lesson.
